planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Louisiana botanist and hybridizer Caroline Dormon bred Wheelhorse from 'Rose Of Abbeville' x 'Violet Ray', producing rose-pink standards over brilliant amaranth-rose falls in a classic bitone pattern. Long regarded as one of the most influential parent plants in Louisiana iris breeding, it earned the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1958 after first collecting an Honorable Mention. Grow it in full sun with consistently moist to wet soil, where its vigorous rhizomes multiply readily into sizable clumps.

common_name: Black Widow Louisiana Iris (Spidery Near-Black Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: W. B. MacMillan introduced Black Widow with a blackish-purple self so deep it reads darker than nearly any comparable color-chart plate, carried on a narrow, spidery flower form with no contrasting signal patch. The cultivar's dramatic near-black color and tall late-season stalks earned it the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1968, and it later became an important parent behind darker-flowered Louisiana hybrids such as Bajazzo. Site it in full sun with steady moisture, and give it room at the back of a bog bed since mature stalks can tower well above 4 feet.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Mary Dunn bred Rhett from 'Creole Flame' x 'Monument', producing large, slightly ruffled mahogany red standards and velvety mahogany red falls accented by a fine yellow line crest. It is one of four Dunn introductions to win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal, taking the honor in 1991 after earlier Honorable Mention and Award of Merit recognition. Plant it in full sun with rich, consistently wet soil for the strongest color saturation on its upright stems.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Bred by Mary Dunn from 'Blue Shield' x 'Black Widow', Bajazzo produces deep red-violet standards over velvety red-violet falls that darken further toward the center. It progressed from an Honorable Mention through an Award of Merit before capturing the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 1992, one of four national medals earned by Dunn's introductions. Grow it in full sun with continuously moist to wet soil, and expect early to midseason bloom on sturdy, well-branched stalks.

common_name: Professor Neil Louisiana Iris (Tetraploid Dark Red Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Louisiana State University researcher Joseph Mertzweiller developed Professor Neil as part of his decades-long program converting Louisiana irises to tetraploid chromosome counts, resulting in a dark red self with a large, brilliant yellow signal and a faint musky fragrance. The cultivar climbed from a Cordon Bleu award through an Award of Merit to win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 1999. Give it full sun and steady moisture, and expect the thicker-textured blooms typical of Mertzweiller's tetraploid 'Professor' series.

common_name: Professor Jim Louisiana Iris (Tetraploid Red-Violet Veined Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Another of Joseph Mertzweiller's tetraploid 'Professor' introductions, Professor Jim bears medium red flowers veined in dark red-violet around a yellow signal, with the same faint musky scent found across the series. It moved from an Award of Merit to the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 1996, recognizing the added flower substance that tetraploidy brought to Louisiana iris breeding. Plant it in full sun with consistently wet soil, where its early-midseason stalks reach some of the taller heights in the 'Professor' line.

common_name: Kay Nelson Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Lavender-Pink Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Marvin Granger registered Kay Nelson with light lavender-pink standards over medium to deep lavender-pink, ruffled falls set off by a light greenish-yellow signal. Its compact stature and clean pastel color helped it win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1995. Grow it in full sun with shallow standing water or steadily moist soil, where its shorter midseason stalks suit smaller pond edges and mixed border plantings better than taller Louisiana cultivars.

common_name: Voodoo Magic Louisiana Iris (Fuchsia Purple Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Henry Rowlan bred Voodoo Magic from 'Black Gamecock' x 'Dr. Dormon', producing fuchsia-purple standards and falls brightened by a large yellow spray signal and matching fuchsia styles and crests. After earning a High Commendation, Honorable Mention, and Award of Merit, it went on to win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 1997. Site it in full sun with rich, constantly moist soil for its early-midseason bloom and vivid, saturated purple color.

common_name: Ila Nunn Louisiana Iris (White Iris with Yellow Crest)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Charles Arny registered Ila Nunn as a clean white self, its ruffled white edges set off by a bright yellow line crest running down each fall. The cultivar's crisp, pure coloring made it a popular parent for later white and near-white Louisiana breeding, and it earned the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1972. Grow it in full sun with consistently wet soil, where its late-midseason stalks contrast well against darker purple and red bayou irises nearby.

common_name: Delta King Louisiana Iris (Terra Cotta Red Self)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Ben Hager registered Delta King as a terra cotta red self, a warm brick-orange tone that stood out among the cooler purples and blues common in Louisiana iris breeding of its era. After Honorable Mention and Judges' Choice recognition, it won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1971. Plant it in full sun with steady moisture, and expect midseason bloom on stalks well suited to the middle of a mixed bog planting.

common_name: Eolian Louisiana Iris (Tall Classic Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Charles Arny bred Eolian from 'Louise Arny' x 'New Offering', producing a ruffled, classic light blue self with a small yellow crest that helped define the pure blue color class in Louisiana irises. It earned the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1976 after an earlier Honorable Mention. Grow it in full sun with consistently wet soil, where its tall midseason stalks work well toward the back of a bog garden or pond margin.

common_name: Mrs. Ira Nelson Louisiana Iris (Mineral Violet Self)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Charles Arny named this violet self, bred from 'Louise Arny' x 'G. W. Holleyman', for the wife of Ira Nelson, the LSU horticulturist who helped popularize Louisiana iris breeding. Large triangular yellow crests set off the solid mineral-violet standards and falls, and the cultivar collected an Exhibition Certificate and repeat Judges' Choice honors before winning the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1973. Site it in full sun with rich, constantly moist soil for midseason to late bloom.

common_name: Katherine L. Cornay Louisiana Iris (Tall Violet Self)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Charles Arny registered Katherine L. Cornay as a solid mineral-violet self carried on some of the tallest stalks among his introductions, reaching well above the typical Louisiana iris clump. It won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1969 and was later used as a breeding parent for other violet-toned Louisiana cultivars. Grow it in full sun with steady moisture, and give it staking room since its height can exceed nearby companion plantings.

common_name: Bryce Leigh Louisiana Iris (Pale Lavender Self)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Frank Chowning bred Bryce Leigh as a silvery, pale lavender self that intensifies toward a narrow gold line signal bordered by a thin maroon line on each fall. The subtle, opalescent color combination earned it the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1981. Plant it in full sun with consistently wet soil, where its midseason blooms pair well against the more saturated reds and purples common among Chowning's other Louisiana introductions.

common_name: This I Love Louisiana Iris (Rose-Pink Fading Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Frank Chowning's This I Love opens a deep orchid-rose and quickly softens to a sweet, pale pink self, with lemon-yellow crests and green-tinged style arms adding a two-tone effect as each bloom ages. The distinctive color shift helped it win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1979. Grow it in full sun with rich, continuously moist soil, and expect the color transformation to happen within the first day a flower is open.

common_name: G. W. Holleyman Louisiana Iris (Tall Soft Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: R. Holleyman registered G. W. Holleyman as a soft blue self accented by an orange-yellow midrib that pales to white toward the throat, carried on some of the tallest stalks in the class. Its imposing late-season height and clean color helped it earn the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1966, and it went on to parent other Arny-line Louisiana hybrids, including 'Mrs. Ira Nelson'. Site it in full sun with wet, boggy soil and ample staking room, since mature stalks can reach 5 feet or more.

common_name: Monument Louisiana Iris (Warm White Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Mary Dunn's Monument bears lightly ruffled, warm white flowers with a yellow signal and creamy style arms, a softer alternative to the cooler, pure-white Louisiana cultivars introduced before it. It won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1984, one of four national medals earned by Dunn's introductions, and later became a parent of the medal-winning 'Rhett'. Grow it in full sun with continuously moist to wet soil for strong midseason bloom.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Sam Rix bred Frances Elizabeth as a purplish-bronze self with a dark mulberry-purple spine through the standards and a clear gold signal on the falls, an unusual bronze tone for its era. The cultivar's story became a well-documented chapter in how Louisiana irises spread from Gulf South breeding programs to growers overseas, and it won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1965. Plant it in full sun with steady moisture, where its compact, late-blooming stalks suit smaller garden beds.

common_name: W. B. MacMillan Louisiana Iris (Red Bitone Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Sidney Conger registered W. B. MacMillan as a red bitone with a chrome-yellow signal, notable in its day as one of the first Louisiana iris cultivars bred with distinctly overlapping flower parts for a fuller form. It won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1964 and remains one of the foundational older cultivars still referenced in Louisiana iris breeding history. Grow it in full sun with consistently wet soil for reliable midseason bloom.
